question: What is a Skill in ChatGPT?
answers: A plugin that adds new data sources
A reusable workflow taught once
A model trained for one job
A shared chat history for a team
fact: Teach a task once instead of re-explaining it every time: a small package with a name and description, step-by-step instructions and any supporting files.

question: Which analogy fits a Skill best?
answers: A new chef joining the kitchen team
A locked pantry of ingredients
A phone line to the supplier
A recipe card in a kitchen binder
fact: The chef doesn't memorise every recipe. They scan the index of titles, and when an order matches, they pull the card and follow it exactly.

question: Which file usually holds a Skill's step-by-step instructions?
answers: A file named INSTRUCTIONS.json
A file named WORKFLOW.yaml
A file named SKILL.md
A file named PROMPT.txt
fact: SKILL.md is a plain-text Markdown file with the purpose, inputs, numbered steps, output format and final checks: the method on the card.

question: A Skill's name and description help the assistant decide when to use it.
fact: They are the title in the binder's index. The assistant reads them to decide whether a request matches.

question: How can you call a Skill explicitly?
answers: By @-mentioning it in the chat
By turning on a model setting
By re-uploading it each time
By asking an admin to run it
fact: Besides automatic matching, you can pick one yourself by @-mentioning it when you know exactly which workflow you want.

question: A Skill gives ChatGPT access to apps and data it could not reach before.
fact: A Skill only instructs the assistant how to use the tools and apps it already has. It grants no new data access, which is a handy answer to a security question.

question: A team asks which task is the best candidate for a Skill. Best answer?
answers: A one-off question about a news story
A single idea for a team off-site
A monthly pack with fixed steps
A quick translation of one email
fact: Create a Skill for tasks you repeat, with several steps, strict formatting or policies, where consistency matters. For a one-off, a plain prompt will do.

question: Which belongs in a Skill's supporting resources?
answers: Templates, examples and scripts
The user's past chat messages
The model's training dataset
The billing records for the team
fact: Beside SKILL.md a Skill can carry templates, examples, brand guidelines, schemas or scripts: the photo of the finished dish and the special utensils.

question: A Skill's description just says 'Helps with work'. What is likely?
answers: It will fire on every request
It will run correctly but quite slowly
It will be blocked by the admin
It rarely gets matched to requests
fact: The description is how the assistant recognises when to use the Skill. A vague one is the most common reason a Skill never fires, so say what it does and when.

question: In the open Agent Skills format, what is always loaded?
answers: The full instructions of each Skill
Just the short name and description
Every supporting file and script
The last output from each Skill
fact: That is progressive disclosure as the open Agent Skills format works: full instructions load only on a match. OpenAI confirms the description's role but not the loading detail.

question: A team working toward one goal wants shared files and chats. What fits?
answers: A Skill with fixed numbered steps
A Project with shared files and chats
Fine-tuning on the team's chats
A longer system prompt for each person
fact: A Project holds shared context, files and chats for an outcome. A Skill packages a repeatable procedure. Project for the goal, Skill for the routine.

question: Which tool changes what the model knows from your documents?
answers: A Skill, which stores your documents
A prompt, which retrains the model
A Project, which edits the weights
RAG, retrieving from your documents
fact: RAG changes what the model can look up; a Skill changes which procedure it follows. They combine well: the Skill sets out the monthly pack, retrieval supplies the figures.

question: Same steps and format every time, by next week. Best fit?
answers: A Skill with steps and a template
A fine-tune on thousands of examples
A bigger model with higher reasoning
A vector index of past reports
fact: Fine-tuning changes the weights and needs lots of examples. A Skill writes the procedure down in plain files you can edit today, so try it first.

question: How should a team shape its Skills?
answers: One huge Skill that covers everything
One per person, without sharing
Small, combinable ones for each task
Only Skills that run on a schedule
fact: Small Skills are easier to describe, test and combine. One giant workflow gets hard to match and hard to fix.

question: A customer asks who controls who can create, share and install Skills. Best answer?
answers: Whoever wrote each Skill
Each team member, privately
The workspace admins or owners
OpenAI sets it for everyone
fact: Workspace owners and admins decide who can create, use, share and install Skills, depending on plan and settings. Check the current admin options before quoting them.

question: A customer asks, 'Is a Skill just a saved prompt?' Best reply?
answers: More: steps, templates and scripts
Yes, exactly that and nothing more
No, it is a separately trained model
No, it is a database of past answers
fact: A saved prompt is text. A Skill can bundle instructions with templates, examples, brand guidelines or scripts, and the assistant picks it when the request fits.

question: In a monthly pack Skill, which step is the best final check?
answers: Rewrite the title in a bolder style
Add a longer introduction at the start
Email it to the whole company
Check each number traces to a source
fact: Good Skills end with checks. Here every figure traces back to the source file, so whoever runs the pack gets the same trustworthy result.

question: What is the difference between a Skill and a connector?
answers: Skills add access; connectors add steps
Skills add steps; connectors add access
Both add the same knowledge differently
Connectors are admin-only, Skills aren't
fact: A connector links the assistant to an app like Drive. A Skill tells it what to do with what it can reach. Access versus procedure.

question: Which of these is a way to create a Skill in ChatGPT?
answers: Filing a request with OpenAI
Fine-tuning on past outputs
Describing it in a chat
Renaming a saved conversation
fact: There are three ways: with chat, in the editor, or by uploading one. Uploads are scanned and may be marked Needs Review or Blocked.

question: Why does it matter that SKILL.md is plain text in an open format?
answers: It cannot be edited by staff
It can be shared and versioned
It runs faster than other files
It is locked to one product
fact: Because a Skill is plain text in the open Agent Skills format, it can be reviewed, versioned and shared, and reused in tools that support the format.

question: A Skill works when @-mentioned but never fires on its own. First fix?
answers: Sharpen its description
Add more supporting files
Raise the reasoning effort
Fine-tune on its outputs
fact: The steps clearly work, so the matching is the problem. Say what the Skill does and when to use it, in the words people actually use when they ask.

question: How would you show a customer a Skill is worth keeping?
answers: Count how often it gets installed
Ask the model to rate its own output
Check the instructions are detailed
Measure time saved against a baseline
fact: Same as any pilot: agree a measure and baseline first, then compare time saved and rework on real runs. Install counts alone can mislead.

question: A Skill can include a template so every output follows the same layout.
fact: Templates, examples and checklists sit in the Skill's supporting resources, so the output comes out in the house style whoever runs it.

question: Which Skill name will be easiest for an assistant to match?
answers: General reporting assistant
Team workflow helper
Everyday office tasks
Monthly ops review pack
fact: The name and description are what the assistant uses to recognise a Skill. Clear, specific words that match how people ask make it easier to find.

question: A Skill fires on requests it was never meant for. First fix?
answers: Delete the supporting files
Raise the reasoning effort
Add more example outputs
Tighten its description
fact: A description that is too broad matches too much. Say what the Skill does, and what it does not, in the words people use.

question: Several Skills are installed. How does an agent choose one?
answers: It times each Skill on the request
It matches names and descriptions
It uses the most recently added one
It reads every file in every Skill
fact: The name and description are how the assistant recognises when a Skill applies. How it loads the rest varies by tool, so do not promise internals to a customer.

question: Where should long reference material for a Skill live?
answers: Packed into the description line
Repeated in every chat message
In the supporting files
Squeezed into the Skill's name
fact: Keep the description short, since it is how the Skill is recognised, and put detail in supporting files such as templates, examples and references.

question: Why are uploaded Skills scanned before use?
answers: To translate them into other languages
To convert them into fine-tunes
To count how many steps they have
To catch unsafe or unwanted content
fact: A Skill can carry scripts and instructions, so uploads are checked and may be marked for review or blocked. Admins also control who can create, share and install.

question: A Skill's output keeps missing the format. What helps most?
answers: Make the description much longer
Add an example and a final check
Remove the template to cut clutter
Rename the Skill to something punchy
fact: A worked example shows the target, and a closing check step catches drift from it before the answer goes out.

question: Two Skills have near-identical descriptions. What may happen?
answers: Both run at the same time forever
The agent may pick the wrong one
The older one is deleted
Neither can be @-mentioned
fact: Matching rests on descriptions, so overlap causes mix-ups. Give each Skill a distinct job and say when not to use it.

question: A policy changed but the Skill's steps did not. What's the risk?
answers: The Skill stops working altogether
Everyone keeps following old steps
It updates its steps by itself
Users are warned automatically
fact: Consistency cuts both ways. Give each Skill an owner and a review date so the recipe card stays current.

question: Staff need answers from 400 policy PDFs. Best tool?
answers: RAG over the policies
A Skill per policy
Fine-tuning on the PDFs
A longer prompt
fact: This is a knowledge problem: the model needs the right passages. A Skill adds steps, not knowledge, so retrieval is the better fit.

question: Which job is a Skill poor at?
answers: Repeating a review checklist
Making the model know new facts
Producing a standard report layout
Following steps in a set order
fact: A Skill packages how to do a task. Facts come from files, retrieval or connectors, so pair a Skill with those when you need both.

question: Which Skill is mainly about conventions and standards?
answers: One that applies the house report style
One that fetches today's share price
One that stores last year's reports
One that trains on staff chats
fact: OpenAI's page groups Skills into reusable processes, tool-based workflows, and conventions such as a house style or structure. This one enforces a convention.

question: A task changes shape every time, with no fixed steps. Skill?
answers: Yes, Skills adapt to any kind of task
Yes, after fine-tuning
Only if it uses RAG
Probably not: nothing repeats
fact: A Skill captures a repeatable way of working. If each run differs, there is little to write down, and a good prompt each time will do.

question: What should a good Skill description say?
answers: What it does and when to use it
Who built it and when
Every step set out in full detail
Its file size and format
fact: The description helps the assistant decide when the Skill fits, so it should say the job and the situation. The detailed steps belong in the Skill itself.

question: What helps most when asking ChatGPT to draft a Skill?
answers: The topic and a friendly tone
A link to the team's intranet
Task, inputs, steps and format
Last year's reports, unlabelled
fact: OpenAI suggests describing the job, inputs, numbered steps, output format with examples, and quality checks, then reviewing and refining the draft before installing.

question: What should a Skill say about inputs?
answers: Nothing; the model simply guesses it
Only the file name
What the user must supply first
Which model wrote it
fact: Naming the needed inputs, such as a data export or a period, stops the Skill starting work with gaps and inventing the rest.

question: A Skill starts writing before it has the data. Fix?
answers: Make the description much shorter
Rename the Skill
Add more templates
Add an input-check step first
fact: An early step asks for anything missing before drafting. That is cheaper than correcting a polished report built on guesses.

question: What makes an output format instruction clear?
answers: Named sections in a fixed order
A warning to be extra careful here
The word "professional"
A request to stay brief
fact: Concrete structure beats adjectives. Naming each section and its order leaves little room for the layout to drift between runs.

question: A good final check for a customer-email Skill?
answers: Check it is long enough for the topic
Check facts and dates match sources
Check it sounds warm and enthusiastic
Check it opens with a name
fact: A last step that verifies facts catches the errors that matter. Style checks are fine, but accuracy against the source is the one customers notice.

question: Will a Skill make every output identical?
answers: Yes, the steps fix every word
Yes, if the description is clear
No: more consistent, not identical
Only at the highest reasoning effort
fact: Following the same steps and template makes results far more alike, but wording can still vary between runs. Add a final check and review samples.

question: Security asks: does adding a Skill widen what staff can reach?
answers: Yes, it opens all workspace files
Yes, but only for admins
Only with a long description
No: data access is set elsewhere
fact: A Skill adds steps and format, not new data access. What people can reach comes from their permissions and connectors, which admins control.

question: Before a team-written Skill is shared widely, what should happen?
answers: Review it and test real examples
Nothing; Skills are harmless text
Wait for a new model release
Rename it after the team
fact: Shared Skills shape work for many people, and some can include scripts. A review and a test on real cases catches mistakes and unsafe content.

question: A shared Skill holds a process that changes yearly. Who should look after it?
answers: Whoever happened to use it last week
A named owner with a review date
The model itself
No one; it fixes itself
fact: Skills go stale quietly. An owner and a review date keep the steps in line with the process people actually follow.

question: Best first Skill for a sales team?
answers: A rule for every possible deal type
One that rewrites the CRM
A call-notes summary, set format
A one-off research brief
fact: Frequent, structured and easy to check: the team sees value fast and can judge the output against a known layout.

question: What makes a good first Skill candidate?
answers: Rare, creative and very hard to judge
Urgent and different each time
Sensitive and needing no review
Frequent, rule-based, easy to check
fact: Start where steps repeat and results are easy to verify. A small, visible win builds trust before riskier workflows.

question: A colleague built a great Skill. How does the team get it?
answers: Paste its text into every chat
Wait for OpenAI to roll it out
Share it, if settings allow
Each person rebuilds it themselves
fact: Skills can be shared with a workspace or installed on others' behalf if workspace settings allow it. Owners control who can create, use, share and install.

question: The team pastes the same 200-word prompt every day. Better?
answers: Fine-tune a model on that prompt
Make it a Skill with a template
Build a RAG pipeline
Shorten it to one line
fact: Repeated pasting is the signal. A Skill holds the steps and layout once, so everyone starts from the same version.

question: A bot must use changing documents and a fixed format. Combine?
answers: Fine-tuning for both
A Skill with all the documents inside
RAG for facts, a Skill for format
A longer system prompt only
fact: Match each tool to its job: retrieval brings current knowledge, and a Skill supplies the repeatable steps and layout.

question: A firm wants a cheaper model for one narrow task. Is a Skill the tool?
answers: Yes, Skills shrink models
Yes, Skills cut token prices a lot
Only with RAG added
No: fine-tuning or distillation
fact: A Skill changes the instructions, not the model. Making a smaller model do a narrow job well is the work of fine-tuning or distillation.

question: How should a team test a new Skill?
answers: Run it on real past examples
Read its description aloud
Run it once on an easy sample
Ask the model if it works
fact: Real examples reveal gaps in steps and format. Compare outputs with known good ones, and try near-miss requests to check it does not misfire.

question: The steps rarely change but the numbers do. Where do numbers go?
answers: Into the Skill description
Supplied each run, not fixed
Into the model by fine-tuning
Left out; the model recalls them
fact: Keep the Skill about the method and pass current data in each time. Hard-coded figures go stale while everyone trusts the tidy output.

question: A Skill with clear steps can help a junior follow the usual team process.
fact: A Skill writes the team method down once, so newer staff get the same steps and layout as experienced colleagues.

question: The more steps a Skill has, the better it works.
fact: Extra steps add places to go wrong. Keep only the steps that matter, and split a long process into smaller Skills.
